You can, but only with approval. It isn't off limits.

- The normal deploy window is Monday to Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific. Friday deploys need approval from the on-call engineering manager [1]. The October 2026 pipeline changes kept this rule as it was [2].
- Plan for the longer canary. Since October 12, every deploy sits in canary for 45 minutes before it can be promoted automatically [2]. A typical non-data-plane change reaches all cells about 50 minutes after merge. A data-plane change (`ingest/` or `runner/`) takes about two and a half hours [2]. A Friday afternoon deploy can therefore finish late in the day.
- Rollbacks are allowed at any time without approval [1][2].

Also check these:
- **Ledger:** the month-end billing freeze bars normal changes to Ledger from the last business day of the month until invoices go out, usually the 2nd [3]. Today is Saturday, October 31, so the freeze is active until about November 2 [5].
- **Sensitive areas:** changes to billing, authentication and the data plane need two approvals [2].
- **Incidents:** during an incident, the incident commander can approve skipping the canary bake with `/deploy expedite` [2].
- **Holiday freeze:** from December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, only standard and emergency changes ship [3].

No. Taking the name out doesn't make it allowed.

Halcyon's approved AI tools policy says "'De-identified' is not a loophole." Removing a name doesn't make a case non-identifiable, so you have to treat any patient details as PHI [1]. The HIPAA policy says never to put PHI into AI tools that aren't on the approved list [3]. Public chatbots and general-purpose AI assistants are not approved on any device, including personal phones [1].

**What you can use instead:**
- **Quillon Ambient** drafts visit notes from the conversation. It's limited to the Riverside and Elm Park pilot clinics. It needs the patient's verbal consent at the start of every visit, and you must review and sign every note [1].
- **Meridian draft replies** drafts portal message responses inside the EHR. You must edit or approve each one before it's sent [1].
- **Halcyon Assist** is not allowed for this. It's for policy questions only, and you shouldn't paste patient details into it even without names [1][4].

**If you want a new tool approved:** email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui). The tool needs a security risk assessment, a signed business associate agreement, an entry in the systems inventory, and a CMIO clinical safety review for clinical use. This typically takes 6–10 weeks [1].

**17 lab results** from Bayline Reference Laboratories were filed into the wrong patient's chart at the Riverside and Northgate clinics between July 21 and 23, 2026 [1]. The root cause analysis (RCA-26-07) classed it as a Level 2 adverse event [1].

**Why it happened**
- On July 20, Bayline changed its results feed and moved the medical record number (MRN) into a different HL7 segment. It gave no notice [1].
- From July 21, Switchyard, Halcyon's interface engine, couldn't find the MRN and fell back to its secondary matching rule [1].
- That rule matched on last name and year of birth only. It had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume [1].

The RCA lists three root causes [1]:
1. The fallback matching rule was weak.
2. Nothing monitored unmatched or fallback-matched messages. No one was alerted that 100% of Bayline results were using the fallback.
3. The Bayline agreement didn't require advance notice of feed format changes.

**Impact and resolution**
- A medical assistant at Riverside noticed on July 23 that a potassium result didn't match the patient's history. The charge nurse then stopped the feed [1].
- Two patients with abnormal results that went to another chart had follow-up delayed by four and six days. Neither had lasting harm [1].
- All 17 results were moved to the correct charts by July 24. The feed was restored that day with the MRN mapping corrected [1].

**Corrective actions** [1]
- The name-and-birth-year fallback has been removed. Unmatched results now go to a manual work queue (done).
- An alert now fires when more than 1% of a lab's results in an hour use a fallback match (done).
- Amending the lab services agreement to require 30 days' notice of feed changes is in progress. It is due Dec 31.
- Adding a positive patient identification check before results are released to the patient portal is in progress. It is due Nov 30.

Halcyon's deadline is much longer than yours. It's **45 calendar days**, not five business days.

- **Deadline:** The root cause analysis (RCA) for a Level 1 or Level 2 event must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].
- **Start of the clock:** The RCA team is chartered by Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) within 72 hours [1].
- **Immediate escalation:** For a sentinel event, the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1].
- **Review:** Completed RCAs and their action plans go to the Patient Safety Committee. The Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Kenji Watanabe, chairs it. It meets monthly and tracks action items to closure [1].

Halcyon's documents don't use the title "incident commander." The person who does that job is the **charge nurse** on shift. The charge nurse coordinates the immediate response to a patient safety event. That means assigning who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures the equipment, medications or records involved [1].

Who fills the role depends on the clinic:
- **Large clinics:** a designated charge nurse is always on shift, and that person coordinates the response to any patient safety event [2].
- **Medium and small clinics:** a charge nurse is designated whenever two or more RNs are on shift. Otherwise the clinic manager fills the role [2].
- **Any clinic with no charge nurse on shift:** staff tell the clinic manager instead [1].

The charge nurse also has these duties:
- **Notifying the medical director:** for a sentinel event, the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1].
- **Disclosure:** the attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1].

Before any of this, staff first make the patient safe by following the clinical escalation protocol, which includes calling 911 if needed [1].

Halcyon Health gives a defined amount of annual leave. Northwind Labs gives a flexible policy with a minimum.

**Halcyon Health (annual leave policy, effective Oct 1, 2026)**
- Full-time staff get 20 days a year in years 1–3 and 25 days a year from year 4 [6].

**Northwind Labs**
- PTO is flexible, with a minimum of 15 days a year that people are expected to take [1].
- If you're paged for more than 3 hours between 22:00 and 07:00, you take the next morning off without needing approval [2].

**Comparison**
- Halcyon's 20–25 days is a guaranteed amount. Northwind's 15-day figure is only a floor, so actual time off may be higher.
- Halcyon has carry-over and payout rules and a fixed holiday count. The Northwind documents I found don't cover carry-over, holidays or sick leave.
- Halcyon requires advance notice, with the lead time depending on role. I found no equivalent Northwind rule.

I couldn't find Northwind's holiday or sick-leave policies, so a full comparison would need those.

Halcyon uses a business associate agreement (BAA) where you'd use a DPA. It also requires a security risk assessment. Nothing in the sources mentions a "DPA" by name.

**Required before any PHI is shared with a vendor**
- **A signed BAA.** A vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI for Halcyon is a business associate. The BAA must be signed before any PHI is disclosed. That includes test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [5].
- **A security risk assessment.** Any tool or system that will handle PHI needs one [2]. New systems that will hold PHI also need one before go-live [1].
- **An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.** This is also required before go-live [1][2]. The HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) maintains the inventory [1].
- **A clinical safety review by the CMIO.** This applies only to clinical use [2].

**Process and timing**
- Email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) to start [2].
- Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly spent waiting on the BAA [2].

**Examples**
- **Coriander Media:** The BAA was executed on August 18, 2026, and the security risk assessment was completed in August 2026 [4].
- **Tallgrass Survey Co.:** The security risk assessment passed with conditions. The BAA is not executed because Tallgrass wants to keep identifiable responses for 5 years and Halcyon will accept 18 months. So no PHI can go to Tallgrass yet, and the order form is on hold [5].

Northwind has a close equivalent: "Emergency access to customer workspaces" [1]. It covers customer data in software workspaces, not patient charts. It is stricter than Halcyon's break-the-glass process on approval and duration.

| | Halcyon break-the-glass (Meridian EHR) | Northwind emergency access |
|---|---|---|
| What it opens | Patient charts outside your normal treatment, payment or operations relationship [5] | A customer's workspace, for urgent fixes such as a pipeline dropping data, a misconfigured connector or a customer lockout [1] |
| Trigger | Genuine patient-care need, such as an unscheduled walk-in, coverage for a colleague, or telehealth escalation [5] | An open support case or declared incident only. Every request must cite the case or incident ID [1] |
| Approval | None in the moment, because patient care comes first [5] | A second engineer from the support or on-call rotation must approve in Teleport. The approver can't be the requester or be on the same case [1] |
| Justification | Pick a reason and type a short free-text justification [5] | Case or incident ID passed to `nwctl access request` [1] |
| Duration | Until the end of your shift, up to 12 hours [5] | 2 hours, deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport session. You request again if you need more time [1][2] |
| Scope of action | Not specified in the source | Read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent in the case [1] |
| Review | Privacy Officer's team reviews every event within 2 business days. Your manager is asked if the reason is unclear [5] | Sessions are recorded and kept for 1 year. Security reviews a weekly sample and every session that used write access [1] |
| Notification | Not specified in the source | The customer's audit log records the access. Enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours [1] |
| Prohibited uses | Checking on family, coworkers, public figures or yourself [5] | Looking at the workspace of someone you know personally, exporting payloads, or sharing or screen-sharing your session [1] |
| Misuse | Treated as a privacy incident, with sanctions up to termination [5] | Report unexpected data in `#security-help` immediately [1] |

**Main difference:** Halcyon trusts the clinician at the moment of care and reviews afterward. Northwind requires a second person to approve before access starts, and it also reviews afterward. Northwind's controls fit its general rule against standing production access, so even normal Teleport production access expires after 8 hours [2].

No. Neither company allows it for its most sensitive data. Each does permit less sensitive material in Slack.

**Halcyon Health**
- Protected health information (PHI) is never allowed in Slack. The systems inventory says "Never, including DMs" [1].
- The HIPAA policy says PHI may live only in the EHR, the practice management system and approved Halcyon systems. It names Slack as a place PHI must never go [2].
- Use the EHR's secure messaging for patient communication. Use `[secure]` encrypted email for outside providers [2].

**Northwind Labs**
- Restricted data is never allowed in Slack. This class covers customer event payloads, credentials and encryption keys. The policy says it "never leaves production; never in tickets or Slack" [4].
- During emergency access to customer workspaces, don't paste payloads into Slack, tickets or support replies. Use field names and counts instead [5].
- Confidential data covers financials, contracts and employee data. The policy says it's shared on a need-to-know basis, and it doesn't name Slack for this class [4].
- Internal data, such as roadmaps and handbooks, can be shared freely inside Northwind [4].
- Public data has no restrictions [4].
- I found no document that explicitly approves Slack for Confidential data. If you're unsure, ask in `#security-help` [4].

**Reporting a mistake**
- At Northwind, report suspected incidents in `#security-help` or at security@northwind.example. Good-faith reports aren't penalized [4].
- I found no Halcyon incident-reporting steps in these results. Halcyon's privacy contact is privacy@halcyon.example [3].

rows.answer:
You need sign-off from the **change approver of the team that owns the service**. Driftwood is the service whose lifecycle rules do the deleting. The approver is listed in the engineering team directory and the service catalog. Changing these rules is a "normal change" under the production change approval policy [1][2].

Some changes need more than that:
- **Security:** If the service holds Restricted data, you also need the Head of Security or the security on-call delegate. The service catalog marks which services are Restricted. Request `@northwind/security` as a reviewer [1].
- **ADR:** Any change to how long customer data is kept needs an ADR linked from the PR [1].
- **Customer notice:** If you shorten retention, the account team must give 30 days' notice to Enterprise customers whose contracts reference a retention period [1].
- **Longer retention:** The standard allows Enterprise customers to contract for up to 730 days, but only with security team approval [2].

**Process**
1. Add the `change:normal` label to the PR and fill in the risk and rollback sections [1].
2. Request review from the approver or their delegate as a CODEOWNERS reviewer [1].
3. Ship within 7 days of approval, or re-request it [1].

The holiday freeze runs December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, and only standard and emergency changes are allowed during it [1].

The documents don't name the specific team or approver for the Driftwood archive buckets. Check the service catalog for that. The retention standard is owned by Security (Tomasz Wierzbicki), and questions go to `#security-help` [2][4].

rows.answer:
Changing when medication reminder texts go out is a **significant change**, because reminders are patient-facing automation [1]. It needs all three of these approvals [1]:

1. **System steward approval.** I'm assuming the reminders belong to Digital Health Engineering – Patient Engagement, whose steward is Felix Brandt [1]. The sources don't say which team owns the reminder system, so confirm that first. If another team owns it, that team's steward approves instead.
2. **Clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao.** Her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei, can give it in her place [1].
3. **Review at the Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB).** It meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [1].

The project lead brings the change to CSCAB as a change request with a CHG number [4]. CSCAB sets the go-live date [4].

If the change moves the reminder job to a different runner or server, you also need a written runbook. It must state how double-running is prevented [1]. This rule came from IR-0412, when two reminder runners were active at once and patients got duplicate reminders [1][3].

CSCAB can defer a change if the CMIO or her delegate withholds sign-off. On October 28, the refill-acknowledgement message was deferred for this reason [2].

rows.answer:
An Enterprise workspace can use reference tables of up to **500 million rows**. Growth is capped at 50 million rows [1]. This comes from the product spec's goals, so it is a design target. I didn't find a document confirming that the limit is enforced as shipped.

Some related limits and caveats:
- Tributary is still in private beta, and general availability is targeted for January 2027 [3].
- Rebuilding a 50M-row snapshot takes about 25 minutes today, and Enrich steps on that partition stall while it runs [2]. RFC-031 proposes persisted snapshots to cut restore time to under 90 seconds, but it is not yet fully approved [2]. Rebuild times for tables much larger than 50M rows weren't in the documents.
- Each runner partition has a 2 GiB memory budget for reference state. Partitions that would exceed it spill to disk rather than fail [2].
- Joins against tables that change more than 1,000 times per second are out of scope [1].
- Enterprise can force a snapshot rebuild through the API once every 2 minutes [4].

A pin (a Hydrant "hold") can stay in place for at most **4 hours**. After that, Hydrant takes over scaling again [1].

- Set the pin with `nwctl hydrant hold --cell <cell> --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`. The `--ttl` value in that example is 2 hours, but the cap is 4 hours [1].
- Holds are standard changes, so they need no approval [1].
- To release a hold early, run `nwctl hydrant release --cell <cell>` [1].
- Don't use `nwctl scale ingest` to pin the count. Hydrant treats the replica count as its own and reverts manual changes within 2 minutes [1].
- The older on-call runbook still tells you to scale with `nwctl scale ingest` [3]. The Hydrant launch notes say Hydrant replaces that scaling step [1].

rows.answer:
The API returns **HTTP 429** when a workspace goes over its rate limit. The response includes a `Retry-After` header that gives the number of seconds to wait before retrying [1].

- **SDKs:** Northwind's SDKs honour `Retry-After` automatically and back off exponentially [1]. Customers on a custom HTTP integration have to read the header and wait themselves.
- **Limit scope:** Limits apply per workspace, not per API key, so ten keys in one workspace share one budget [1].
- **Bursts:** Short bursts of up to 2x the limit are allowed for 10 seconds [1].
- **Quota:** Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [1].
- **Plans without an endpoint:** An endpoint that isn't available on the customer's plan returns **HTTP 403**, not 429 [1]. A customer who sees a 403 has a plan problem, not a rate-limit problem.

Limits vary by endpoint and plan. For example, `POST /v2/events` allows 100 req/s on Starter, 2,000 on Growth and 10,000 on Enterprise [1].

Enterprise customers can get ingest limits raised up to 3x the default by contract. The Data Plane on-call can grant temporary raises of up to 72 hours for a one-off backfill [1].

Ask in the `#eng-leads` Slack channel. The codename register is maintained by Mateo Alvarez (Group PM) [1].

Naming rules from the register [1]:
- **No collisions.** The name can't match a production service name, a vendor name, or an existing codename.
- **Internal use only.** Codenames must never appear in customer-facing material, release notes, or the status page.

Check the register before you pick a name. It lists the active codenames: Tributary, Lantern, Hydrant, Undertow, Sandbar, Tidepool, Bellbuoy and Wayfinder. It also lists the retired ones, Keel and Gannet [1]. Production service names to avoid include Conduit, Driftwood, Keystone, Ledger, Atlas, Beacon, Lookout, `runner` and `ingest-gateway` [4].

I found no other rules, such as a required theme or format. Most existing names are nautical or water-related, but the register doesn't say that's a requirement.

Normally Harriet Vance (approver) or Arjun Mehta (delegate) would sign off, but both are out November 24–27, so neither can approve on November 25.

**Who normally approves:** A normal change needs sign-off from the change approver of the team that owns the service [1]. Identity & Billing (IDB) handles Ledger. Harriet Vance is the approver and Arjun Mehta is the delegate [3]. The IDB status notes confirm that both are out November 24–27 [4].

**Your options:**
- **Get approval before November 24, or after they return.** This is the cleanest route. Approvals are valid for 7 days, so approval given on or after November 18 would still be valid if the change ships on November 25 [1].
- **Ask the VP Engineering.** If the approver and delegate are both unavailable, Dmitri Sokolov (VP Engineering) may approve. The exception gets logged in `#eng-changes` [1][3].

**Other requirements:**
- Add the `change:normal` label to the PR. Fill in the risk and rollback sections. Request the approver or delegate as a CODEOWNERS reviewer [1].
- If your change touches a Restricted service, you also need Head of Security (Tomasz Wierzbicki) or security on-call sign-off. Request `@northwind/security` [1]. The catalog notes say Ledger never stores card numbers [2]. I didn't find Ledger's classification, so check the service catalog.
- November 25 is not in a freeze. The month-end billing freeze starts on the last business day of the month, and the holiday freeze starts December 18 [1].

rows.answer:
You need sign-off from **PLAT's change approver**, who is **Oluwaseun Adeyemi**. If he's out, his delegate **Kofi Mensah** can approve [6].

- Hydrant is owned by PLAT, and each cell's floor and ceiling lives in the PLAT infrastructure repo. Changing a ceiling counts as a normal change (infrastructure configuration) [1][4].
- You don't need security sign-off. Hydrant stores no customer data and isn't a Restricted service [1].
- To get approval, add the `change:normal` label to the PR and fill in the risk and rollback sections. Then request review from the approver or their delegate as a CODEOWNERS reviewer. Approval is valid for 7 days [4].

Hydrant pages the Data Plane on-call when a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes. The launch notes say that usually points to a gateway problem rather than real traffic [1]. Check with DP (Priya Raman's team, `#team-dataplane`) before you raise the ceiling. DP owns the gateways [1][6].

If you only need to pin the replica count temporarily, for example while debugging, use `nwctl hydrant hold`. Holds last at most 4 hours and need no approval [1].

rows.answer:
The $1,200/month plan is Growth [1]. On Growth, `POST /v2/events/batch` allows these limits [2]:

- **Rate:** 50 requests per second.
- **Request size:** up to 10,000 events or 10 MB per request.

Other limits that affect a backfill:
- Limits apply per workspace, not per API key, so several keys share one budget [2].
- Bursts up to 2x the limit (100 req/s) are allowed for 10 seconds [2].
- Above the limit, the API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. The SDKs honor it automatically [2].
- Rejected requests don't count against the monthly event quota [2].
- Growth includes 100 million events a month, with overage at $8 per additional million [1]. A year of history may exceed that, so check the event volume.

If the customer needs more throughput, the DP on-call primary can grant a temporary raise for a one-off backfill. It can last up to 72 hours [2]. Growth limits are otherwise fixed by contract. Customers who need more should talk to sales about Enterprise [2].

**You owe them a first response within 2 hours.**

The plan with 100 million events a month is Growth [6]. Pipelines being down is a P1 (Critical) issue [3]. Under the SLA effective August 1, 2026, Growth P1 gets a first response within 2 hours. Coverage is 24/7, and you owe them an update every 4 hours after that [3].

- **Older SLA:** The 2025 edition said 4 hours with updates every 8 hours. It was replaced for tickets opened on or after August 1, 2026, so it doesn't apply [2][3].
- **SLA clock:** It starts when a ticket is opened by email or through the help center. Nothing posted in a Slack Connect channel starts it [2].
- **Priority:** The customer picks the priority when they open the ticket. Support can change it after triage but has to tell the customer why [2].

- `GET /v2/usage`

A deploy now bakes in the canary cell for **45 minutes** before it can be promoted automatically. The October 2026 pipeline change raised this from 20 minutes [1]. The engineering handbook still says 20 minutes, but the pipeline note says it overrides the handbook where they differ [1][2].

Automatic promotion needs all of the following [1]:
- Error rate and p95 latency stay within 10% of the baseline.
- There are no sustained TLS handshake errors between gateways and brokers in canary.
- Runner consumer lag doesn't grow by more than 2 minutes during the bake.

You can change the timing in two ways:
- Anyone can run `/deploy hold <deploy-id>` in Slack to keep a deploy in canary until someone runs `/deploy release` or rolls it back [1].
- During an incident, the incident commander can approve skipping the bake with `/deploy expedite` [1].

Changes under `ingest/` or `runner/` also roll out in waves after canary, with 30 minutes between waves [1].

rows.answer:
**No, don't run `nwctl scale ingest` by hand.** The runbook step is out of date. Hydrant, the ingest gateway autoscaler, replaced it. It has been on in us-west since October 15 [2]. Hydrant treats the replica count as its own and reverts a manual change within 2 minutes [2].

What to do instead:
1. **Find the affected cell on the ingest dashboard.** Then check the gateway TLS handshake errors. These runbook steps still apply [2]. INC-2291 was a TLS handshake failure that looked like a gateway problem [1][3].
2. **Check whether Hydrant is at its ceiling.** If a cell sits at its ceiling for 10 minutes, Hydrant pages the Data Plane primary on-call. That usually means a gateway problem, not real traffic [2]. High CPU together with 5xx errors points the same way.
3. **If you need to pin the replica count**, for example while debugging a bad gateway build, use a hold [2]:
   `nwctl hydrant hold --cell us-west --replicas <n> --ttl 2h`
   - A hold lasts at most 4 hours, then Hydrant takes over again.
   - A hold is a standard change and needs no approval.
   - Release it early with `nwctl hydrant release --cell us-west` [2].
4. **If the ceiling is too low**, raising it is a normal change. It needs sign-off from PLAT's change approver, and the config lives in the PLAT infrastructure repo [2].
5. **If the incident is serious**, declare it with `/incident declare` in Slack [1].

If Hydrant's controller is down, it pages the Platform primary. Gateways keep their last replica count in that case [2].

**Other things to check**
- Discounts are measured against the first-year contract value at list price [2].
- If the customer prepays annually, Growth already gets a 15% discount, which is more than 12% [1][2].
- If the customer is a registered non-profit or an accredited educational institution, they get 50% off automatically, with no approval needed [2].

An Enterprise workspace can force a reference-table snapshot rebuild **once every 2 minutes**. The limit is on `POST /v2/reference-tables/{id}/refresh` [2]. For comparison, Growth gets 1 per 10 minutes, and Starter doesn't have the endpoint [2].

- Limits are per workspace, not per API key, so all keys in a workspace share one budget [2].
- Going over the limit returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header [2].
- A forced refresh discards the runner's snapshot and rebuilds it from a full table scan. That is expensive for large tables, and most customers don't need it because change data capture keeps snapshots current [1].

rows.answer:
No, don't throw them out yet. Halcyon's policy says 10 °C is out of range, and it also says not to discard anything [1]. The fridge must stay between 2 °C and 8 °C [1].

Do these steps:

1. **Label and keep the stock.** Mark the affected vaccines "Do not use". Keep them refrigerated in a working unit. Record the reading, the time and how long it lasted [1].
2. **Call the clinical pharmacist within 1 hour.** The pharmacist checks with the manufacturers on whether the stock can still be used [1].
3. **File a SafeReport.** If no vaccine was given, it's a Level 4 near miss. If a patient received affected vaccine, report at a higher level [1][2]. When unsure, report at the higher level [2].
4. **Give nothing from that stock** until the clinical pharmacist releases it in writing [1].

Frozen vaccines are never refrozen or reused once thawed [1].

The pharmacist's check with the manufacturers decides whether any of it is discarded. The policy doesn't say how long or how far out of range stock can be and still be used. If you're at a non-hub clinic and need replacement stock, Tier 1 items are ordered weekly. Tier 2 items are transferred from the nearest hub within 2 business days [1].

Halcyon's standard is **10 business days** for a patient's request for their own record when it isn't available instantly in the portal [1]. HIPAA allows up to 30 calendar days, but 10 business days is our internal target [1].

- **Fee:** An electronic copy (secure email or encrypted USB) or a paper copy costs a $6.50 flat fee. Fees are waived for patients in the sliding-fee program [1].
- **Unpaid balances:** Never refuse or delay a request because of an unpaid balance [1].
- **Logging:** Log the request in the HIM request queue in Meridian EHR [1].
- **Sensitive records:** Records with extra legal protection, such as substance use treatment records, go out only after the Privacy Officer has reviewed the request [1].
- **Other recipients:** Records sent to another treating provider have a 3-business-day turnaround. Attorney or insurer requests have a 15-business-day turnaround and need a signed authorization [1].

**Probably not today.** Elmhurst can't give the first shingles dose from its own stock.

- The shingles vaccine is the recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV). The formulary lists it as Tier 2, which means only hub clinics stock it [1].
- Elmhurst (ELH) is not a hub clinic. The hubs are Riverside, Northgate and Harbor Point [2].
- A non-hub clinic has to request a transfer from the nearest hub. Transfers arrive within 2 business days [1]. Today is Saturday, and Elmhurst is open 09:00–12:00 [2]. The vaccine is therefore unlikely to arrive before early next week.

**Options**
- Request the transfer now and book the patient for when it arrives.
- Send the patient to a hub clinic that is open today. Riverside is open 08:00–12:00, Northgate until 14:00 and Harbor Point until 16:00 [2]. I don't know whether a given hub has stock on hand today, so call ahead.

**Other details**
- Only an RN or clinician can give RZV, not an MA [1].
- It is for patients aged 50 and over [1].
- It is a 2-dose series, with the second dose 2–6 months after the first [1].
- The self-pay price is $205 per dose. Insured patients are billed to their plan [1].
- Make sure an RN or clinician is on shift at Elmhurst for the visit. The Saturday session minimum includes one RN [5].

Escalate to **Meridian Clinical Systems**. Wren is the Meridian EHR upgrade to release 2027.1 [3].

**P1 response time: 15 minutes.** Meridian support is 24/7 [1]. A P1 means the system is down or unusable at one or more clinics, or the problem creates a patient-safety risk, such as results not arriving [1].

For a scheduled Meridian upgrade, Meridian also staffs a live bridge line with its own engineers for the whole cutover window [1]. During the cutover, use that bridge first. The cutover is scheduled for Saturday, February 6, 2027, starting at 22:00 Eastern, with 6 hours of planned downtime [2].

If Meridian misses the 15-minute P1 response, the Service Desk escalates to Meridian's account manager and tells the owning team's steward [1]. The owning team is CI [1]. Two missed P1 responses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer and recorded in the vendor's annual review [1].

Two related points from the cutover plan:
- The cutover must finish by 04:00 Sunday so verification can happen before Harbor Point's 10:00 clinic opens [2].
- Switchyard is built in-house, so it has no outside vendor. For a Switchyard problem, the Service Desk pages the owning team directly [1]. The reference labs' HL7 feeds are a separate case. Bayline Reference Laboratories' interface desk has a 30-minute P1 response [1].

Four clinics count as large under the staffing standard effective September 1, 2026. A clinic is large if it averages more than 80 visits a day [1]. The bands use the Q3 2026 averages in the October 2026 clinic directory [3]:

| Clinic | Avg visits per day |
|---|---|
| Harbor Point (HBP) | 118 [3] |
| Northgate (NGT) | 102 [3] |
| Riverside (RVS) | 94 [3] |
| Elm Park (ELP) | 85 [3] |

Elm Park would not have been large under the 2025 standard, which set the cutoff at over 90 visits a day [2]. At 85 visits a day, it now counts as large.

The other clinics fall into the medium or small bands:
- **Medium (40 to 80 visits a day):** Northbridge (52) and Riverbend (46) [1][3].
- **Small (under 40 visits a day):** Elmhurst (38) and Cedar Hollow (31) [1][3].

Large clinics must have at least 3 physicians or NPs, 2 MAs per clinician, 2 RNs with one designated charge nurse, and 4 front desk staff [1].

Bands are reset every quarter, so a clinic can change bands when its volume changes [3].

Five vendors give you 24/7 coverage for a P1, according to the vendor support and escalation matrix (updated 2026-10-15) [1]:

|---|---|---|
| Polyglen Interpreting | Interpreter operations desk | 10 minutes |

Systems built in-house have no outside vendor. For these, the Service Desk pages the owning team directly [1].

If a vendor misses its P1 response time, the Service Desk escalates to the vendor's account manager. Two misses in a quarter are reported to the HIPAA Security Officer [1].

**We don't charge anything.** Halcyon eliminated the no-show fee under the revised policy that took effect October 5, 2026 [1].

- The old policy charged a $25 fee from the third no-show in a 12-month period. Medicaid and sliding-fee patients were exempt [2]. The 2026 revision replaces that policy in full [1].
- Unpaid no-show fees billed before October 5, 2026 are waived. Revenue Cycle Management will reverse them on patient statements. Front desk staff shouldn't try to collect them [1].
- A visit now counts as a no-show only if the patient doesn't arrive or join and didn't cancel at least 2 hours beforehand. The old cutoff was 24 hours. Cancelling by replying to an appointment reminder counts as cancelling [1].
- On the third no-show in 12 months, a care coordinator calls the patient to ask about barriers. They can offer ride vouchers, a telehealth visit, a different appointment time, or an interpreter [1].
- Patients are not discharged for no-shows [1].

No. Since September 1, 2026, every clinic, small ones included, must have at least one RN on site during all open hours [1]. Saturday sessions need an RN too [1].

The 2025 standard let small clinics (under 45 visits a day) run without an RN. In those clinics the physician or NP handled triage and the MA gave Tier 1 vaccines [2]. The 2026 standard replaced it [1]. It was changed because small clinics without an RN were sending too many triage calls to the physician [1].

The sources don't give a specific procedure for an RN absence. The general coverage rules cover physician/NP shortfalls only. The standard doesn't say whether the float pool is the fallback for a missing RN, but it does keep 2 RNs on call daily in the float pool [1]. The 2025 standard's escalation steps were to call the float pool, then ask the regional medical director whether to reduce the schedule, and to log any session run below minimum [2]. That standard is superseded, so confirm with Clinical Operations before relying on those steps.

If a site has to close unexpectedly for staffing reasons, the clinic manager tells the telehealth front desk supervisor so in-person visits can be converted to telehealth where clinically appropriate. The manager also posts the closure on the Halcyon app [4].

Halcyon logs patient events in **SafeReport**, the patient safety event reporting system run by QPS (Quality & Patient Safety) [5]. The policy is the "Sentinel and adverse event reporting policy" [1].

**Who files:** Anyone involved in the event or who witnessed it files a report. Reporting is never optional and never punished [1].

**How soon:** The policy puts the immediate steps under a "Within 24 hours" heading. It doesn't give a separate filing deadline for SafeReport, so I can't say more precisely than that. Other timings in the policy:
- First, make the patient safe, then tell the charge nurse on shift. If the clinic has no charge nurse on shift, tell the clinic manager [1].
- For a sentinel event, the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director within **1 hour** [1].
- Every Level 1 and Level 2 event gets a root cause analysis (RCA). QPS charters the RCA team within 72 hours, and the RCA must be finished within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1].

**Related points:**
- The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family. The charge nurse or medical director is present [1].
- QPS decides whether the event must be reported to a state health department or accrediting body, and makes those reports [1].
- Privacy breaches are handled separately. They go to the Privacy Officer [1].
- Events caused by software or patient-facing automation follow the same policy [1].

I didn't look up Northwind's `/incident declare` process, so this answer doesn't compare the two.

rows.answer:
Yes, Northwind reviews incidents in a similar spirit. Its postmortems are blameless, which is the same idea as just culture. The main difference is who writes them.

**Same approach:** Northwind requires a blameless postmortem for every SEV-1 and SEV-2, due within five business days of resolution [4]. Its write-ups focus on system causes and fixes. The INC-2291 postmortem, for example, covers a missing intermediate CA, a canary alert threshold that was too high, and action items with owners [3]. Your policy likewise looks for system causes, not someone to blame [1].

**Who writes it:** At Northwind, the incident commander assigns a postmortem owner when they resolve the incident. That owner is usually an engineer who worked the incident, not a separate investigator or team. In INC-2340, the IC (Kofi Mensah) named Arjun Mehta as postmortem owner, with a due date of Oct 13 [5]. Arjun was the engineer who found and diagnosed the problem [5].

At Halcyon, QPS charters an RCA team within 72 hours, and the RCA is completed within 45 days [1]. A Quality & Patient Safety lead heads each RCA. For RCA-26-07 that was Lorraine Pike [2]. Halcyon's Patient Safety Committee then reviews the RCA [1].

**Review step at Northwind:** Postmortem drafts go to the reliability meeting. INC-2351's draft was circulated Oct 21 and is due for review on Nov 5 [4]. I found no documented standing review committee or independent author role.

**Not required:** SEV-3 incidents don't need a postmortem [4].

Yes. Northwind runs access reviews every quarter. If nobody re-confirms an access grant, the system revokes it automatically.

Each team lead runs the review for their team. Access that isn't re-confirmed is revoked automatically [2]. So a missing sign-off doesn't leave the access in place. The access is removed.

Some related Northwind controls:
- Production access goes through Teleport and expires after 8 hours. Nobody has standing access to production databases [2].
- Access to customer data needs a ticket linked to a support case or incident, and all sessions are recorded [2].
- When someone leaves, all their access is revoked within one hour of their final working time [2].

The "monthly EHR access log review" in your question comes from Halcyon Health's HIPAA policy, not Northwind's [1]. I found nothing about EHR access at Northwind. The Northwind documents I found cover production and customer-data access.

Halcyon doesn't let staff put patient data into an AI tool until the tool is on its approved list. Getting a tool approved usually takes **6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the vendor's business associate agreement (BAA)** [1].

**How to start:** Email the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) at privacy@halcyon.example [1].

**What a tool that handles PHI needs** [1]:
1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed BAA with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory.
4. A clinical safety review by the CMIO, if the tool is for clinical use.

**Other points:**
- No PHI can go to a vendor before the BAA is signed. That includes test files and "just a few names" for a pilot [3].
- Removing a name doesn't make data safe to use. Staff must treat any patient details as PHI [1].
- Public chatbots, browser extensions that summarize pages, meeting transcription apps, and translation apps for clinical conversations are not allowed [1].
- The approved tools today are Quillon Ambient (pilot clinics only) and Meridian draft replies. Halcyon Assist is approved for policy questions only, with no PHI [1].
- Other AI scribes are not approved, even for trials [2].

**How this compares to Northwind:** I only searched for Halcyon's process. I didn't look up Northwind's #vendor-review process, so I can't say how the two differ.

rows.answer:
**Short answer:** If the change is purely cosmetic, the owning team's system steward can approve it alone. It needs no CMIO sign-off and no CSCAB review.

**Who the steward is.** Halcyon's change-control policy gives each owning team one system steward who approves changes to that team's systems [1]. For the patient app, the likely owner is Digital Health Engineering – Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), whose steward is **Felix Brandt** [1]. The projects register lists that team as owner of the app's refill-acknowledgement project, and Felix presented that change at CSCAB [2][4].

**Check who owns bill-pay.** I found nothing saying which team owns the bill-pay screen specifically. Billing is a Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) area, and its steward is Tomás Herrera [1]. Confirm the owner in the systems inventory before you ask for approval. The policy refers to that inventory, but I didn't find it in the search results.

**Why the steward's OK is enough.** The policy classes cosmetic changes as "minor," and minor changes need steward approval only [1].

**Where "cosmetic" could stop applying.** A change is "significant" if it affects any of these [1]:
- patient-facing automation, such as reminders and outreach messages
- the patient app's clinical content
- medication information, orders or results routing
- clinical decision support
- scheduler or job-runner cutovers

A significant change needs all three of the following [1]:
- the steward's approval
- clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate, Dr. Benedict Osei
- review at CSCAB, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 ET

A layout, colour or styling change on bill-pay doesn't touch any of those areas. If your tweak changes wording, messages, or what triggers them, ask the steward whether it still counts as minor.

Changes made without the required approvals are reported to QPS as safety events [1].

**Northwind (INC-2340, October)**

- **Cause:** The payment provider's webhook timed out during the month-end batch. Northwind's retry logic then re-ran the batch, and invoice creation wasn't idempotent [6].
- **Main fix:** Invoice creation now uses an idempotency key per workspace and billing period [6]. It was deployed on October 6, and a dry run of the job showed zero duplicates [6]. The status report lists it as shipped October 8 [8], and the changelog agrees [7].
- **Other follow-ups:**
  - A daily reconciliation report comparing invoices to charges is done [8].
  - An alert for provider webhook timeouts during a billing batch is still open, due November 6 [8].

**Halcyon (IR-0412, September 3)**

- **Cause:** The reminder scheduler moved to a new job runner on September 2. Both the old and new runners were active during the cutover, and neither checked whether a reminder had already been sent [1].
- **Technical fix:** The rules adopted after IR-0412 include an idempotency key on every patient-facing automated message. The projects register states this for the Marigold project and refers to it as part of those post-IR-0412 rules [5]. I didn't find a document that spells out how the key is implemented.
- **Process control:** Any cutover that moves a job between runners or servers now needs a written runbook. The runbook must state how double-running is prevented [2]. Cutovers are also significant changes. They need steward approval, CMIO clinical safety sign-off, and CSCAB review [2].

Both fixes are idempotency keys. Northwind keys on workspace and billing period. Halcyon's source doesn't say what its key is built from. Halcyon also added a cutover runbook requirement, which Northwind's sources don't mention.

rows.answer:
**Northwind Labs has a change freeze. Halcyon Health doesn't.**

**Northwind Labs**
- **Holiday freeze:** December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027. Only standard and emergency changes ship during it [1]. The on-call rota says the same about the December 22 week [3].
- **Month-end billing freeze:** this applies to Ledger only. There are no normal changes from the last business day of the month until invoices go out, usually on the 2nd [1]. It could touch your plans around December 31 to January 2.
- **Rollbacks:** these are allowed at any time, including during freezes [1][2].
- **Normal deploy window:** Monday to Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific. Friday deploys need approval from the on-call engineering manager [2].
- **Pipeline timing:** canary bake time is now 45 minutes, and data-plane changes roll out in waves. A data-plane change takes about 2.5 hours to reach every cell, so allow for that [2].

**Halcyon Health**
- The Juniper steering committee notes say "No IT freeze at Halcyon" [10]. I found no formal freeze policy.
- Clinic managers asked that Juniper pilot training not land in the week of December 21 [10]. That is a request about training, not a freeze on production changes.
- Change control still applies. Significant changes need the system steward's approval, CMIO clinical safety sign-off, and review at CSCAB, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [8]. Significant changes include anything affecting patient-facing automation, orders, results routing, or scheduler and job-runner cutovers [8]. CSCAB sets cutover dates [7]. Plan around its meeting schedule over the holidays. I didn't find a holiday schedule for CSCAB.
- Staff leave for December 20 to January 2 is also contested, because approvals for that period rotate year to year [5]. That could limit who is available for approvals.

- **Who approves:** The incident commander (IC) can approve emergency changes during a declared incident [1]. That includes changes that would normally need the owning team's change approver [2].

- **Related:** The IC can also approve skipping the deploy bake with `/deploy expedite`. The expedite is logged in `#eng-changes` [5].

**Halcyon Health**
- **Who approves:** The on-call medical director may approve emergency changes. These are changes made to stop ongoing patient harm [7]. You reach them through the answering service at 555-0144, option 2 [8].
- **Review afterwards:** The Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB) reviews the change at its next meeting [7]. CSCAB meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [7]. Its decisions are logged in the change register [7]. Changes made without the required approvals are reported to Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) as safety events [7].

**Key differences**
- Northwind's emergency approver is the incident commander, and the review is done by one person, the owning team's change approver, within two business days.
- Halcyon's emergency approver is the on-call medical director, and the review is done by a board at its next meeting.
- Northwind's trigger is a declared incident. Halcyon's is stopping ongoing patient harm.
